extracted.intended_audience: graduate students and researchers in geometric analysis / Ricci flow
extracted.subtask_description: A textbook/chapter exposition of maximum principles, ODE–PDE comparison lemmas, curvature pinching (Hamilton–Ivey), Li–Yau and Li–Yau–Hamilton estimates, and Perelman's conjugate-heat estimate / reduced distance in the analysis of the Ricci flow.

rubrics_metrics.name: ODE maximum-principle propagation (Lemma, first result)
rubrics_metrics.description: If ϕ(t) satisfies a differential inequality of the form dϕ/dt ≤ C ϕ (after replacing ϕ by e^{-Ct}ϕ one may assume dϕ/dt ≤ 0 whenever ϕ(t) ≥ 0) and ϕ(a) ≤ 0 at initial time a, then ϕ(t) ≤ 0 for all t ∈ [a,b].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses a barrier/ε-argument: show ϕ(t) ≤ ε(t−a) for arbitrary ε>0 by contradiction (take largest interval where inequality would hold and extend). This is the elementary ODE version of the maximum principle used repeatedly to deduce nonpositivity/nonnegativity propagation for scalar quantities obtained from PDEs by taking sup/inf or testing against linear functionals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Derivative estimate for a sup-function (Lemma 2.3.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let X be a complete smooth manifold, Y ⊂ X compact, ψ(x,t) smooth on X×[a,b]. Define ϕ(t)=sup_{y∈Y} ψ(y,t). If y∈Y attains the supremum at time t (ψ(y,t)=ϕ(t)), then dϕ/dt ≤ ∂ψ/∂t (y,t).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof via choosing times t_j↘t with maximizers y_j, extracting convergent subsequence (compactness of Y), applying mean value theorem to compare ψ(y_j,t_j)−ψ(y_j,t), and passing to the limit. This lemma bridges ODE arguments and PDEs by allowing pointwise-in-time derivative control of sup-in-space quantities; used to reduce PDE comparison to ODE inequalities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterization of ODEs preserving closed convex sets (Lemma 2.3.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let U⊂R^n open and Z⊂U a closed convex subset. Consider dϕ/dt = N(ϕ,t) with N continuous and Lipschitz in ϕ. The following are equivalent: (i) any solution starting in Z at time t0 remains in Z for later times; (ii) for every ϕ∈∂Z and every t, ϕ + N(ϕ,t) ∈ T_ϕ Z (equivalently for every support linear functional l at ϕ, l(N(ϕ,t)) ≤ 0).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses support functions l for the convex set Z, the distance function s(ϕ)=dist(ϕ,Z) expressed as a sup over support functionals (so Lemma 2.3.3 applies), Lipschitz continuity to estimate derivative of s(ϕ), and Lemma 2.3.2 (ODE maximum principle) to conclude s(ϕ) stays zero. Practical use: to check invariance of convex constraints under an ODE, verify the tangent-cone/support-function condition on the boundary.

rubrics_metrics.name: PDE preservation of convex fiberwise constraints (Theorem 2.3.1 and extension idea)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a PDE solution σ(x,t) (section of a vector bundle) is uniformly bounded and pointwise (fiberwise) takes values in closed convex sets K_x that are invariant under parallel translation and are preserved by the ODE obtained by dropping spatial diffusion, then the PDE solution stays in the bundle-wise set K (i.e., σ(x,t)∈K_x for all x,t) provided initial data lies in K.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The proof combines: (i) reducing to a compact tubular neighborhood, (ii) building a global sup-type function s(t)=sup_x inf_{η∈∂K_x} l_x(σ(x,t)−η)−εe^{At}f(x), (iii) applying Lemma 2.3.3 to differentiate s(t), using Lemma 2.3.4 to control ODE part, estimating diffusion terms via local extensions (parallel translate support vectors) to make Laplacian/nonlinear terms nonpositive at maxima, then applying ODE maximum-principle to deduce s(t)≤0. This is the standard technique to deduce that fiberwise convex ODE-invariance implies PDE-invariance under diffusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time-dependent convex set preservation (Chow–Lu generalization, Theorem 2.3.5)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let K(t)⊂V be closed subsets depending on time satisfying: (H3) K(t) invariant under parallel translation by ∇^t; (H4) in each fiber V_x the set K_x(t) is nonempty, closed and convex for each t; (H5) the space–time track ∪_{t∈[0,T]} K(t)×{t} is closed. If for each x any solution of the ODE in the fiber starting in K_x(t0) stays in K_x(t) for later times, then any uniformly bounded PDE solution σ(x,t) that starts in K(t0) remains in K(t) for later times.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the time-dependent analogue of Theorem 2.3.1; the same strategy (sup-function, Lemma 2.3.3 and Lemma 2.3.4, control of diffusion terms) applies but one must account for the time-dependence of the constraints. The hypotheses (H3)–(H5) are the checklist to verify when applying the result.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hamilton–Ivey curvature pinching estimate (Theorem 2.4.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a complete Ricci-flow solution on a 3-manifold with bounded curvature, if the initial curvature operator eigenvalues λ≥μ≥ν satisfy appropriate lower bounds then at all points/times a pinching estimate holds: the most negative eigenvalue ν is controlled by the scalar curvature R via an inequality of the form R ≥ (−ν)[log(−ν) − const] whenever ν<0 (precise form uses the inverse of f(x)=x(log x −3)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof method: define an explicit closed O(3)-invariant convex set K in the 3×3 curvature-operator space using a convex/concave split (trace linear inequality and inequality involving f^{-1}(trace)), check K is preserved by the ODE system dλ/dt=λ^2+μν, etc. by direct computation, then invoke Theorem 2.3.1 to deduce PDE preservation under Ricci flow. Practical takeaway: negative sectional curvature cannot become too negative relative to positive curvature; this is a quantitative pinching that is fundamental in 3D Ricci-flow singularity analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Li–Yau gradient estimate for heat equation (Theorem 2.5.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: On an n-dimensional complete Riemannian manifold with nonnegative Ricci curvature, any positive solution u(x,t) of ∂u/∂t = Δu satisfies ∂u/∂t − |∇u|^2/u + (n/2t) u ≥ 0 for t>0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stronger quadratic/vector-field form: for any vector field V, ∂u/∂t + 2∇u·V + u|V|^2 + (n/2t)u ≥ 0; taking optimal V=u^{-1}∇u recovers the scalar inequality. Method: compute for log u and apply maximum-principle arguments. Use this inequality to derive Harnack inequalities and heat-kernel bounds by path integration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hamilton's Li–Yau estimate for scalar curvature on surfaces (Theorem 2.5.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let g(t) be a complete Ricci-flow solution on a surface with initial scalar curvature bounded, nonnegative everywhere and positive somewhere. Then the scalar curvature R(x,t)>0 for t>0 and satisfies ∂R/∂t − |∇R|^2/R + R/t ≥ 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof sets L=log R and considers Q = ∂L/∂t − |∇L|^2 = ΔL + R, then uses evolution equations and a maximum-principle argument (analogous to Li–Yau) to show Q + 1/t ≥ 0. Yields Harnack inequalities for R by path-integration. This is the Ricci-flow analogue of Li–Yau in 2D.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harnack inequality for scalar curvature on surfaces (Corollary 2.5.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a complete Ricci-flow solution on a surface with bounded, nonnegative scalar curvature, for any x1,x2 and 0<t1<t2 we have R(x2,t2) (t1/t2) ≥ exp(−d_{t1}(x1,x2)^2 / 4(t2−t1)) · R(x1,t1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derived by integrating the Li–Yau inequality along a space–time path (choose geodesic at time t1 and constant-velocity parametrization). Useful to compare curvature values at different points/times; the metric shrinking property (nonnegative curvature) simplifies estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Li–Yau–Hamilton matrix estimate (Hamilton, Theorem 2.5.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let g(t) be a complete Ricci-flow solution with bounded curvature and nonnegative curvature operator. For any one-form W_a and any two-form U_{ab}, the quadratic quantity Q = M_{ab} W_a W_b + 2 P_{abc} U_{ab} W_c + R_{abcd} U_{ab} U_{cd} is nonnegative everywhere, where M_{ab} = ΔR_{ab} − (1/2)∇_a∇_b R + ... and P_{abc} = ∇_a R_{bc} − ∇_b R_{ac} (precise definitions in text).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sketch: compute evolutions of involved tensors, set up Q and examine its parabolic evolution; at a first zero point extend U,W to force desirable derivative conditions and show evolution yields contradiction unless Q≥0. The matrix inequality implies many scalar monotonicity/Harnack-type consequences (trace and contraction give usual Li–Yau–Hamilton scalar inequalities).

rubrics_metrics.name: Trace Li–Yau–Hamilton inequality and monotonicity (Corollary 2.5.5)
rubrics_metrics.description: For any one-form V^a, ∂R/∂t + R/t + 2∇_a R V^a + 2 R_{ab} V^a V^b ≥ 0. In particular, taking V=0 implies tR(x,t) is pointwise nondecreasing in time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the traced/contraction consequence of the matrix Li–Yau–Hamilton inequality. Use it to obtain local derivative estimates (via Shi-type estimates) and monotonicity properties used in singularity analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local derivative estimates from Li–Yau–Hamilton (Corollary 2.5.6)
rubrics_metrics.description: If at time t>0 the scalar curvature R ≤ M in a ball of radius r around p, and the solution is complete with bounded curvature and nonnegative curvature operator, then for k≥1 one has a bound |∇^k Rm(p,t)| ≤ C_k M^2 (1/r^{2k} + 1/t^k + M^k) for constants C_k depending only on dimension and k.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses monotonicity of tR (so R bounded on a time interval) and the local derivative estimates (Shi-type). This gives control of higher derivatives in regions where curvature is locally bounded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harnack inequality in higher dimensions (Corollary 2.5.7)
rubrics_metrics.description: If g(t) is complete with bounded and nonnegative curvature operator, then for x1,x2 and 0<t1<t2 we have R(x2,t2) (t1/t2) ≥ exp(− d_{t1}(x1,x2)^2 / 2(t2−t1) ) · R(x1,t1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A higher-dimensional analogue of the 2D Harnack, with a different constant in the exponent coming from the matrix estimate and the traced inequality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monotonicity for ancient solutions (Corollary 2.5.8)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a complete ancient Ricci-flow solution (defined on (−∞,T)) with bounded and nonnegative curvature operator, the scalar curvature R(x,t) is pointwise nondecreasing in time: ∂R/∂t ≥ 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument: translate time origin (remove 1/t terms) letting α→−∞ in the Li–Yau–Hamilton inequalities to eliminate the 1/t terms; then trace inequality yields ∂R/∂t ≥ 0. Important when analyzing ancient κ-solutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Li–Yau–Hamilton estimate for Kähler–Ricci flow (Theorem 2.5.9, Cao)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a complete Kähler–Ricci-flow solution with bounded curvature and nonnegative holomorphic bisectional curvature, the Hermitian matrix Q_{α arβ} = ∂R_{α arβ}/∂t + R_{α arγ} R_{γ arβ} + ∇_γ R_{α arβ} V^γ + ∇_{ ar γ} R_{α arβ} V^{ arγ} + R_{α arβγ arδ} V^γ V^{ arδ} + (1/t) R_{α arβ} satisfies Q_{α arβ} W^α W^{ arβ} ≥ 0 for all V and W.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trace/contraction consequences: (i) scalar curvature satisfies the Li–Yau type inequality ∂R/∂t − |∇R|^2/R + R/t ≥ 0; (ii) assuming R_{α arβ}>0, the determinant φ = det(R_{α arβ})/det(g_{α arβ}) satisfies ∂φ/∂t − |∇φ|^2/φ + (n/ t) φ ≥ 0. These extend Li–Yau–Hamilton control to Kähler setting under holomorphic bisectional nonnegativity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perelman's Li–Yau type estimate for conjugate heat equation (Lemma 2.6.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a Ricci-flow g(t) on M for t∈[0,T) and a solution of the conjugate heat equation u = (4πτ)^{-n/2} e^{-f} (with τ=T−t), define H = 2Δf − |∇f|^2 + R + f/τ − n/τ and v = τ H u. Then ∂H/∂τ = ΔH − 2∇H·∇f − (1/τ) H − 2 |R_{ij} + ∇_i∇_j f − (1/2τ) g_{ij}|^2, and ∂v/∂τ = Δv − Rv − 2τ u |R_{ij} + ∇_i∇_j f − (1/2τ) g_{ij}|^2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequences: the nonpositive definite term implies H ≤ 0 (hence Perelman's Li–Yau-type inequality H≤0) and τH is nonincreasing with τ. For the fundamental solution u one gets H ≤ 0 and then, by integrating along space–time paths, an inequality 2√τ f(q,τ) ≤ inf_γ ∫_0^τ √s (R + |γ'|^2/2) ds, which yields Perelman's reduced distance l(q,τ) = (1/2√τ) inf L(γ) and related heat-kernel type estimates. This connects analytic conjugate-heat estimates with the geometric reduced distance used in Perelman's entropy and no-local-collapsing arguments.
